{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name=":1" /> is a philosophical framework developed by Kitaro Nishida, a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>. This framework emerged as Nishida’s critical response to Western ontological assumptions and epistemology. Nishida sought to provide an alternative ontology, grounded in experience and self-awareness, that would unify the subjective and objective within a more comprehensive and concrete conception.<ref name=":0" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name=":1" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]].<ref name=":1" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned the conventional notion of consciousness by considering the reflexivity of self-awareness. He posited that if consciousness did not possess the reflexivity of self-awareness, it would be akin to a mechanical reaction, incapable of accounting for awareness. He argued that self-awareness has a logical structure that connects it to the world of objects.<ref name=":0" />
For Nishida, awareness is structurally self-reflexive. He likens this reflexivity to how an infinite set mirrors itself in its subsets. Nishida contemplated the world as possessing a form of self-awareness through the manner in which it reflects itself in everything that exists within it. In his view, the self-awareness of an individual is a fraction of this larger reflection of the world. He redefined consciousness, presenting it not as a trait specific to an individual, burather as an expansive field that goes beyond the individual, mirroring the world.<ref name=":0" />
.<ref name=":0" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term “Basho” is a Japanese word that translates as “place” or “topos.” In this framework, Nishida explains that there are various 'places' or topoi that consciousness occupies.<ref name=":0" />
He identified a hierarchy of topoi ranging from the most abstract to the more concrete. The most abstract topos is that of universals used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is consciousness, which Nishida termed as the topos of relative nothingness, as it is a no-thing relative to the objects of consciousness. This is followed by the topos of reflexive self-awareness, where acts such as seeing, knowing, and desiring take place. At a higher level, there is the topos of the “intelligible world,” where the creative self pursues values like truth, beauty, and goodness. Nishida eventually considers the ultimate topos to be that of absolute nothingness, which defies description and predication.<ref name=":0" />
== Me-Ontology == Parallel to the logical schema of topoi, Nishida presented an ontological perspective which he referred to as a 'me-ontology'. This term derives from the Greek word 'meon,' meaning non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative nothingness, or consciousness, is in contrast to the topos of being. The absolute nothingness is seen as underlying both, transcending the distinction. Nishida utilized the Japanese term ‘[[zettai]]’, meaning absolute, but also connoting the breaking through or overcoming of opposition, to illustrate this.<ref name=":0" />

{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name=":1" /> is a philosophical framework developed by Kitaro Nishida, a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>. This framework emerged as Nishida’s critical response to Western ontological assumptions and epistemology. Nishida sought to provide an alternative ontology, grounded in experience and self-awareness, that would unify the subjective and objective within a more comprehensive and concrete conception.<ref name=":0" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name=":1" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]].<ref name=":1" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned the conventional notion of consciousness by considering the reflexivity of self-awareness. He posited that if consciousness did not possess the reflexivity of self-awareness, it would be akin to a mechanical reaction, incapable of accounting for awareness. He argued that self-awareness has a logical structure that connects it to the world of objects.<ref name=":0" />
For Nishida, awareness is structurally self-reflexive. He likens this reflexivity to how an infinite set mirrors itself in its subsets. Nishida contemplated the world as possessing a form of self-awareness through the manner in which it reflects itself in everything that exists within it. In his view, the self-awareness of an individual is a fraction of this larger reflection of the world. He redefined consciousness, presenting it not as a trait specific to an individual, burather as an expansive field that goes beyond the individual, mirroring the world.<ref name=":0" />
.<ref name=":0" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term “Basho” is a Japanese word that translates as “place” or “topos.” In this framework, Nishida explains that there are various 'places' or topoi that consciousness occupies.<ref name=":0" />
He identified a hierarchy of topoi ranging from the most abstract to the more concrete. The most abstract topos is that of universals used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is consciousness, which Nishida termed as the topos of relative nothingness, as it is a no-thing relative to the objects of consciousness. This is followed by the topos of reflexive self-awareness, where acts such as seeing, knowing, and desiring take place. At a higher level, there is the topos of the “intelligible world,” where the creative self pursues values like truth, beauty, and goodness. Nishida eventually considers the ultimate topos to be that of absolute nothingness, which defies description and predication.<ref name=":0" />
== Me-Ontology == Parallel to the logical schema of topoi, Nishida presented an ontological perspective which he referred to as a 'me-ontology'. This term derives from the Greek word 'meon,' meaning non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative nothingness, or consciousness, is in contrast to the topos of being. The absolute nothingness is seen as underlying both, transcending the distinction. Nishida utilized the Japanese term ‘[[zettai]]’, meaning absolute, but also connoting the breaking through or overcoming of opposition, to illustrate this.<ref name=":0" />

{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name=":1" /> is a philosophical framework developed by Kitaro Nishida, a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>. This framework emerged as Nishida’s critical response to Western ontological assumptions and epistemology. Nishida sought to provide an alternative ontology, grounded in experience and self-awareness, that would unify the subjective and objective within a more comprehensive and concrete conception.<ref name=":0" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name=":1" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]].<ref name=":1" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name=":0" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name=":0" />
.<ref name=":0" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "place" or "topos." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name=":0" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is consciousness. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include truth, beauty, and goodness. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute nothingness. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name=":0" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative nothingness is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name=":0" />

== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "place" or "topos." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name=":0" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is consciousness. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include truth, beauty, and goodness. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute nothingness. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name=":0" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative nothingness is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name=":0" />

{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name=":1" /> is a philosophical framework developed by Kitaro Nishida, a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>. This framework emerged as Nishida’s critical response to Western ontological assumptions and epistemology. Nishida sought to provide an alternative ontology, grounded in experience and self-awareness, that would unify the subjective and objective within a more comprehensive and concrete conception.<ref name=":0" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name=":1" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]].<ref name=":1" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name=":0" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name=":0" />

== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "place" or "topos." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name=":0" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is consciousness. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include truth, beauty, and goodness. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute nothingness. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name=":0" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative nothingness is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name=":0" />

{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name=":1" /> is a philosophical framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>. This framework emerged as Nishida’s critical response to Western ontological assumptions and epistemology. Nishida sought to provide an alternative ontology, grounded in experience and self-awareness, that would unify the subjective and objective within a more comprehensive and concrete conception.<ref name=":0" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name=":1" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]].<ref name=":1" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name=":0" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name=":0" />
.<ref name=":0" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "place" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name=":0" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name=":0" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name=":0" />

Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "place" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a philosophical framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>. This framework emerged as Nishida’s critical response to Western ontological assumptions and epistemology. Nishida sought to provide an alternative ontology, grounded in experience and self-awareness, that would unify the subjective and objective within a more comprehensive and concrete conception.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]].<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a philosophical framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>. This framework emerged as Nishida’s critical response to Western ontological assumptions and epistemology. Nishida sought to provide an alternative ontology, grounded in experience and self-awareness, that would unify the subjective and objective within a more comprehensive and concrete conception.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]].<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "place" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a [[Philosophy|philosophical]] framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>. This framework emerged as Nishida’s critical response to Western ontological assumptions and epistemology. Nishida sought to provide an alternative ontology, grounded in experience and self-awareness, that would unify the subjective and objective within a more comprehensive and concrete conception.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]].<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "place" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a [[Philosophy|philosophical]] framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>. This framework emerged as Nishida’s critical response to Western ontological assumptions and epistemology. Nishida sought to provide an alternative ontology, grounded in experience and self-awareness, that would unify the subjective and objective within a more comprehensive and concrete conception.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]].<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "[[place|place]]" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a [[Philosophy|philosophical]] framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>.
At its basic level the Logic of Basho is an idea of a hierarchical system of reality where each level or "place" envelops and determines the nature of the levels below it. The ultimate reality, according to Nishida, is "absolute nothingness," a source of infinite potentiality and creativity beyond being and non-being.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
It marked a departure from traditional Western philosophy by Kitaro Nishida.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]],<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> or "place".<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "[[place|place]]" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a [[Philosophy|philosophical]] framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>.
At its basic level the Logic of Basho is an idea of a hierarchical system of reality where each level or "place" envelops and determines the nature of the levels below it. The ultimate reality, according to Nishida, is "absolute nothingness," a source of infinite potentiality and creativity beyond being and non-being.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
It marked a departure from traditional Western philosophy by Kitaro Nishida.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]],<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> or "place".<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topoi hierarchy == Nishida proposed this hierarchy iof topoi
# The Place of Direct Experience: Nishida starts with "pure experience." This is a simple state where there's no split between the person feeling and the thing felt. Here, everything is just experienced directly, without thinking about who is experiencing or what is being experienced. # The Place of Conscious Self-Awareness: Next, he talks about self-awareness (自覚, jikaku). This is where the mind looks at itself. It's like when you think about your thinking. This place is about the mind knowing itself and what it's aware of at the same time. # The Place of Objective Reality:This is the outside world we relate to. Analogous to the [[Phenomenology|phenomenological]] world of Immanuel Kant. # The Place of the Historical World: This level is about people living together through time. It includes how people act, how they express themselves, and how they live with others in society. It's about the big picture of human life and history. # The Place of Absolute Nothingness: Finally, Nishida introduces the idea of absolute no-thingness (絶対無, zettai mu). This is a reality past normal human experience.
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "[[place|place]]" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a [[Philosophy|philosophical]] framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>.
At its basic level the Logic of Basho is an idea of a hierarchical system of reality where each level or "place" envelops and determines the nature of the levels below it. The ultimate reality, according to Nishida, is "absolute nothingness," a source of infinite potentiality and creativity beyond being and non-being.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
It marked a departure from traditional Western philosophy by Kitaro Nishida.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]],<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> or "place".<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topoi hierarchy == Nishida proposed this hierarchy iof topoi
# The Place of Direct Experience: Nishida starts with "pure experience." This is a simple state where there's no split between the person feeling and the thing felt. Here, everything is just experienced directly, without thinking about who is experiencing or what is being experienced. # The Place of Conscious Self-Awareness: Next, he talks about self-awareness (自覚, jikaku). This is where the mind looks at itself. It's like when you think about your thinking. This place is about the mind knowing itself and what it's aware of at the same time. # The Place of Objective Reality:This is the outside world we relate to. Analogous to the [[Phenomenology|phenomenological]] world of Immanuel Kant. # The Place of the Historical World: This level is about people living together through time. It includes how people act, how they express themselves, and how they live with others in society. It's about the big picture of human life and history. # The Place of Absolute Nothingness: Finally, Nishida introduces the idea of absolute no-thingness (絶対無, zettai mu). This is a reality past normal human experience.
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "[[place|place]]" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a [[Philosophy|philosophical]] framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>.
At its basic level the Logic of Basho is an idea of a hierarchical system of reality where each level or "place" envelops and determines the nature of the levels below it. The ultimate reality, according to Nishida, is "absolute nothingness," a source of infinite potentiality and creativity beyond being and non-being.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
It marked a departure from traditional Western philosophy by Kitaro Nishida.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]],<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> or "place".<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topoi hierarchy == Nishida proposed this hierarchy iof topoi
# The Place of Direct Experience: Nishida starts with "pure experience." This is a simple state where there's no split between the person feeling and the thing felt. Here, everything is just experienced directly, without thinking about who is experiencing or what is being experienced. # The Place of Conscious Self-Awareness: Next, he talks about self-awareness (自覚, jikaku). This is where the mind looks at itself. It's like when you think about your thinking. This place is about the mind knowing itself and what it's aware of at the same time. # The Place of Objective Reality:This is the outside world we relate to. Analogous to the [[Phenomenology|phenomenological]] world of Immanuel Kant. # The Place of the Historical World: This level is about people living together through time. It includes how people act, how they express themselves, and how they live with others in society. It's about the big picture of human life and history. # The Place of Absolute Nothingness: Finally, Nishida introduces the idea of absolute no-thingness (絶対無, zettai mu). This is a reality past normal human experience.
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "[[place|place]]" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

revision.text:

{{Kyoto School}}
{{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a [[Philosophy|philosophical]] framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>.
At its basic level the Logic of Basho is an idea of a hierarchical system of reality where each level or "place" envelops and determines the nature of the levels below it. The ultimate reality, according to Nishida, is "absolute nothingness," a source of infinite potentiality and creativity beyond being and non-being.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
It marked a departure from traditional Western philosophy by Kitaro Nishida.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]],<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> or "place".<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "[[place|place]]" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida proposed this hierarchy of topoi # The Place of Direct Experience: Nishida starts with "pure experience." This is a simple state where there's no split between the person feeling and the thing felt. Here, everything is just experienced directly, without thinking about who is experiencing or what is being experienced. # The Place of Conscious Self-Awareness: Next, he talks about self-awareness (自覚, jikaku). This is where the mind looks at itself. It's like when you think about your thinking. This place is about the mind knowing itself and what it's aware of at the same time. # The Place of Objective Reality:This is the outside world we relate to. Analogous to the [[Phenomenology|phenomenological]] world of Immanuel Kant. # The Place of the Historical World: This level is about people living together through time. It includes how people act, how they express themselves, and how they live with others in society. It's about the big picture of human life and history. # The Place of Absolute Nothingness: Finally, Nishida introduces the idea of absolute no-thingness (絶対無, zettai mu). This is a reality past normal human experience.
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Kyoto School}} [[File:Nishida's hierarchy of Topoi.svg|thumb|Nishida's hierarchy of Topoi]] {{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a [[Philosophy|philosophical]] framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>.
At its basic level the Logic of Basho is an idea of a hierarchical system of reality where each level or "place" envelops and determines the nature of the levels below it. The ultimate reality, according to Nishida, is "absolute nothingness," a source of infinite potentiality and creativity beyond being and non-being.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
It marked a departure from traditional Western philosophy by Kitaro Nishida.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]],<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> or "place".<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "[[place|place]]" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida proposed this hierarchy of topoi # The Place of Direct Experience: Nishida starts with "pure experience." This is a simple state where there's no split between the person feeling and the thing felt. Here, everything is just experienced directly, without thinking about who is experiencing or what is being experienced. # The Place of Conscious Self-Awareness: Next, he talks about self-awareness (自覚, jikaku). This is where the mind looks at itself. It's like when you think about your thinking. This place is about the mind knowing itself and what it's aware of at the same time. # The Place of Objective Reality:This is the outside world we relate to. Analogous to the [[Phenomenology|phenomenological]] world of Immanuel Kant. # The Place of the Historical World: This level is about people living together through time. It includes how people act, how they express themselves, and how they live with others in society. It's about the big picture of human life and history. # The Place of Absolute Nothingness: Finally, Nishida introduces the idea of absolute no-thingness (絶対無, zettai mu). This is a reality past normal human experience.
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Kyoto School}} [[File:Nishida's hierarchy of Topoi.svg|thumb|Nishida's hierarchy of Topoi]] {{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a [[Philosophy|philosophical]] framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>.
At its basic level the Logic of Basho is an idea of a hierarchical system of reality where each level or "place" envelops and determines the nature of the levels below it. The ultimate reality, according to Nishida, is "absolute nothingness," a source of infinite potentiality and creativity beyond being and non-being.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
It marked a departure from traditional Western philosophy by Kitaro Nishida.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]],<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> or "place".<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "[[place|place]]" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida proposed this hierarchy of topoi # The Place of Direct Experience: Nishida starts with "pure experience." This is a simple state where there's no split between the person feeling and the thing felt. Here, everything is just experienced directly, without thinking about who is experiencing or what is being experienced. # The Place of Conscious Self-Awareness: Next, he talks about self-awareness (自覚, jikaku). This is where the mind looks at itself. It's like when you think about your thinking. This place is about the mind knowing itself and what it's aware of at the same time. # The Place of Objective Reality:This is the outside world we relate to. Analogous to the [[Phenomenology|phenomenological]] world of Immanuel Kant. # The Place of the Historical World: This level is about people living together through time. It includes how people act, how they express themselves, and how they live with others in society. It's about the big picture of human life and history. # The Place of Absolute Nothingness: Finally, Nishida introduces the idea of absolute no-thingness (絶対無, zettai mu). This is a reality past normal human experience.
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Kyoto School}} [[File:Nishida's hierarchy of Topoi.svg|thumb|Nishida's hierarchy of Topoi]] {{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a [[Philosophy|philosophical]] framework developed by [[Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida]], a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the [[Kyoto School|Kyoto School]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>.
At its basic level the Logic of Basho is an idea of a hierarchical system of reality where each level or "place" envelops and determines the nature of the levels below it. The ultimate reality, according to Nishida, is "absolute nothingness," a source of infinite potentiality and creativity beyond being and non-being.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
It marked a departure from traditional Western philosophy by Kitaro Nishida.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as [[Topos (disambiguation)|topos]],<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> or "place".<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "[[place|place]]" or "[[topos|topos]]." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is [[consciousness|consciousness]]. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include [[truth|truth]], [[beauty|beauty]], and [[goodness|goodness]]. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute [[nothingness|nothingness]]. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida proposed this hierarchy of topoi # The Place of Direct Experience: Nishida starts with "pure experience." This is a simple state where there's no split between the person feeling and the thing felt. Here, everything is just experienced directly, without thinking about who is experiencing or what is being experienced. # The Place of Conscious Self-Awareness: Next, he talks about self-awareness (自覚, jikaku). This is where the mind looks at itself. It's like when you think about your thinking. This place is about the mind knowing itself and what it's aware of at the same time. # The Place of Objective Reality:This is the outside world we relate to. Analogous to the [[Phenomenology|phenomenological]] world of Immanuel Kant. # The Place of the Historical World: This level is about people living together through time. It includes how people act, how they express themselves, and how they live with others in society. It's about the big picture of human life and history. # The Place of Absolute Nothingness: Finally, Nishida introduces the idea of absolute no-thingness (絶対無, zettai mu). This is a reality past normal human experience.
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative [[nothingness|nothingness]] is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '[[zettai]].' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />

{{Kyoto School}} [[File:Nishida's hierarchy of Topoi.svg|thumb|Nishida's hierarchy of Topoi]] {{Nihongo|The Logic of Basho|場所の論理|Basho no ronri}}<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> is a {{ill|Philosophy|philosophical|en}} framework developed by {{ill|Kitaro Nishida|Kitaro Nishida|en}}, a prominent Japanese philosopher and founder of the {{ill|Kyoto School|Kyoto School|en}}<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-20 |title=THE LOGIC OF BASHO |url=https://archive.ph/wip/e1Ab1 |access-date=2023-06-07 |website=The Kyoto School of Philosophy |language=en}}</ref>.
At its basic level the Logic of Basho is an idea of a hierarchical system of reality where each level or "place" envelops and determines the nature of the levels below it. The ultimate reality, according to Nishida, is "absolute nothingness," a source of infinite potentiality and creativity beyond being and non-being.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
It marked a departure from traditional Western philosophy by Kitaro Nishida.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
The term Basho no Ronri is a slightly less formal phrasing. Ronrigaku is the term for formal logic and ronri is a more informal term.<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> Basho is sometimes translated as {{ill|Topos (disambiguation)|topos|en}},<ref name="www.rep.routledge.com" /> or "place".<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Self-Awareness and World == Nishida questioned how people think about consciousness. He focused on self-awareness. He believed self-awareness was key to understanding consciousness. He said that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mechanical reaction. It would not explain awareness. He claimed that self-awareness has a logical structure. This structure links it to the world of objects..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida saw awareness as self-reflexive. He compared it to an infinite set reflecting in its subsets. He thought the world had self-awareness. This is because it reflects in everything that exists. Nishida believed individual self-awareness is part of this larger reflection. He changed how people think about consciousness. He did not see it as just an individual trait. He saw it as a wide field. This field extends beyond the individual. It mirrors the world..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
.<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
== Topos and the Logic of Place == The term "Basho" is Japanese. It means "{{ill|place|place|en}}" or "{{ill|topos|topos|en}}." Nishida used this term in his work. He said consciousness occupies different 'places' or topoi..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida created a hierarchy of topoi. They range from abstract to concrete. The most abstract topos is universals. These are used in judgments or propositions. The next topos is {{ill|consciousness|consciousness|en}}. He called this the topos of relative nothingness. It is a 'no-thing' compared to the objects of consciousness. After this is the topos of reflexive self-awareness. This is where seeing, knowing, and desiring happen. Above this is the topos of the "intelligible world." Here, the creative self seeks values. These values include {{ill|truth|truth|en}}, {{ill|beauty|beauty|en}}, and {{ill|goodness|goodness|en}}. Nishida saw the ultimate topos as absolute {{ill|nothingness|nothingness|en}}. This topos is beyond description and predication..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
Nishida proposed this hierarchy of topoi # The Place of Direct Experience: Nishida starts with "pure experience." This is a simple state where there's no split between the person feeling and the thing felt. Here, everything is just experienced directly, without thinking about who is experiencing or what is being experienced. # The Place of Conscious Self-Awareness: Next, he talks about self-awareness (自覚, jikaku). This is where the mind looks at itself. It's like when you think about your thinking. This place is about the mind knowing itself and what it's aware of at the same time. # The Place of Objective Reality:This is the outside world we relate to. Analogous to the {{ill|Phenomenology|phenomenological|en}} world of Immanuel Kant. # The Place of the Historical World: This level is about people living together through time. It includes how people act, how they express themselves, and how they live with others in society. It's about the big picture of human life and history. # The Place of Absolute Nothingness: Finally, Nishida introduces the idea of absolute no-thingness (絶対無, zettai mu). This is a reality past normal human experience.
== Me-Ontology == Nishida had a logical view of topoi. He also had an ontological perspective. He called this 'me-ontology.' This term comes from the Greek word 'meon.' 'Meon' means non-being. The topos of being describes the natural world. The topos of relative {{ill|nothingness|nothingness|en}} is consciousness. It contrasts with the topos of being. Absolute nothingness underlies both. It transcends their differences. Nishida used the Japanese term '{{ill|zettai|en}}.' This means absolute. It also suggests breaking through or overcoming opposition. He used this term to explain his idea..<ref name="Maraldo-2019" />
